failure-reconstructed.title: Why Qantas Flight 32's Engine Exploded
lines: Qantas Flight 32 suffered an uncontained engine failure.
In seconds, debris tore through the wing and cut wiring.
The crew spent nearly two hours working through failures, then landed safely.
The cause was a small oil pipe inside the engine.
It had been machined off-centre, leaving its wall too thin.
A fatigue crack leaked oil, which caught fire.
A turbine disc overheated and burst.
Engines with the faulty pipe were inspected and replaced.

impossible-brief.title: What If a Teaspoon of Neutron-star Matter Appeared on Earth?
lines: Why one teaspoon of neutron star would explode.
It weighs about 900 Great Pyramids.
Neutron stars pack 1.4 Suns into about 10 kilometres.
Squeeze Earth that hard, and it fits in 305 metres.
Outside the star, that matter wouldn't stay compressed.
Freed from crushing gravity, it would expand violently.
So the teaspoon isn't a weight. It's a bomb.

critical-thread.title: Why a Cut Cable Needs a Ship to Fix It
lines: Your internet depends on hidden seabed cables.
Deep-sea sections are only about 25 millimetres across.
They weigh around 1.4 tonnes per kilometre on the seabed.
Continents were already wired this way by 1872.
When one breaks, a cable ship must find the fault and splice it at sea.
Until then, traffic reroutes onto other cables, if they have room.
So repair ships are part of the internet too.
